title: NASA's Asteroid Hunter Passes a Key Test: NEO Surveyor's Giant Sunshade Powers Up
excerpt: NASA reports that solar-array testing is complete for NEO Surveyor, the infrared space telescope that will hunt for asteroids big enough to threaten Earth.
content:
NASA's next planetary-defense telescope has cleared a major hardware hurdle. The agency said October 26 that teams have finished functional and performance testing of NEO Surveyor's solar array — the largest component of a spacecraft designed to find asteroids large enough to threaten Earth before they find us.

The array is unusual: it is also the spacecraft's sunshade. A single structure, 6 metres tall and 2.4 metres across its base, combines two solar panels set at a 23.5-degree angle with the shade that protects the telescope's infrared detectors. The array carries 864 solar cells and can generate up to 2 kilowatts — all of the spacecraft's electricity — while shielding detectors that must stay cold enough to measure the faint heat of distant asteroids.

That heat measurement is the mission's advantage. A large, dark asteroid can look like a smaller, shiny one in reflected sunlight. Measuring infrared heat helps scientists tell size from reflectivity — the difference between a rock that would burn up and one that would not.

The cooling design matters for the mission's lifespan. Instead of finite cryogen supplies that limited earlier infrared surveys, NEO Surveyor relies on passive cooling at its observing post near the Sun-Earth L1 point, where the shade blocks solar glare. Two infrared detector arrays, each producing a 16-megapixel mosaic of the sky, will scan in two bands so scientists can estimate an object's temperature and size.

The mission's goal — and its limits

The baseline requirement is to find and characterize at least two-thirds of potentially hazardous asteroids larger than 140 metres within five years of starting its survey. An extended goal, requiring 10 to 12 years of operations, would push completeness past 90%. The launch is planned for no later than June 2028, according to Caltech's IPAC center, which will process and archive the survey data.

Ground tests, however, prove only that the hardware works on Earth. NASA's update gives no date for the next integration milestone — when the tested sunshade joins the complete telescope — and no measured in-orbit sensitivity or discovery rate. The telescope still has to survive launch, reach L1, and keep its detectors cold in space before a single asteroid is found.

Still, the milestone is real: the power and shade system that the entire mission depends on has passed its tests. For a planet that has been hit before, and will be again, that is the kind of quiet engineering news worth noting.
